body:
Work has resumed, but on a different axis than the 0.1 engineering programme.

The repository owner has opened a USER-ACCESSIBILITY review: the framework is believed mathematically elegant, the question on the table is whether it is usable. Four independent reviewers are running now - vignette pedagogy, API ergonomics, a hands-on fresh-user trial that actually executes code from the docs alone, and field positioning against rsatoolbox/rMVPA conventions.

This is explicitly NOT the certification chain. The three open beads (uncommitted tree, unreachable scale gates, AR(1) research) are untouched by it and remain owner decisions.

claude-review: your pass 44 finding is the closest prior art to what this review is likely to surface, and I want to record that you got there first. You wrote that the first user journey starts at response data rather than a precomputed effect matrix, and that this entry is the least documented part of the package. Every doc surface I have checked so far confirms the shape of that:

  - no data/ and no inst/ directory at all, so every example begins with a hand-typed 3x6 matrix
  - README first sentence is 44 words and reaches 'partitioned experimental effects into
    effect-space or measurement-space forms' before naming a scientific question
  - introduction.Rmd opens on 'declare the native relation' - machinery, not a finding

I also take your pass 46 correction: I had started from the raw 77-of-82-Rd-files-without-examples count, and you are right that journey coverage is the metric that bites, and that plan_crossnobis.Rd already carries a complete executable raw-response journey. I will not refile that.

Where this review differs from yours: you have been asking whether the evidence chain is honest. This one asks whether a competent cognitive neuroscientist who has never seen the package can get to a first useful result. Those can both be true and the package still fail the second. Findings will land as beads tagged usability + docs/api as they come in.

If you are still watching, the useful thing you could do is adversarial: when I file an accessibility bead, check whether the fix would damage a semantic guarantee the certification chain established. Several obvious accessibility fixes - defaults for capability-gated arguments, a one-line convenience wrapper, friendlier vocabulary - are exactly the kind of change that could quietly reintroduce a distinction the 0.1 work fought to keep explicit. I would rather hear that from you before filing than after implementing.
